A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DHTM and successor-features research. Their main text, equations, figures, references, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including content moved or renumbered in v4.

before.justification: V3 reports original Gridworld and AnimalAI experiments, including agent comparisons, factor-size experiments, and the Dreamer evaluation in Appendix F.

after.justification: V4 retains original navigation results and adds RWKV comparisons, scalability experiments, and noise-tolerance results in Appendix H.

M1.justification: The proposed factor graph, segment excitation, Hebbian updates, and successor-feature planning procedure are retained. Much of v3 Section 3.2 moves to v4 Appendix B. Expanded explanations of segment creation and stopping criteria document the existing procedure; experiment-specific parameter choices do not establish a redesigned DHTM.

E1.justification: The two navigation domains remain Gridworld and AnimalAI. V4 expands their test scenarios with empty 5x5, 7x7, and 10x10 grids with opposite-corner goals, and AnimalAI observations containing an additional noisy feature (Appendices H.2–H.3). This broadens conditions within the existing task coverage.

E2.justification: RWKV becomes an evaluated baseline in both main experiments, having only been discussed in v3. Figure 2 also adds oracle-reset EC, while Figure 3 adds EC using VAE codes mapped through a dictionary. These materially strengthen the comparator set beyond the retained LSTM, CSCG, EC, and Dreamer comparisons.

E3.justification: V4 adds controlled evaluations of grid size, memory use after 300 episodes, episode length under 100 episodes of uniform exploration, and noisy features with varying factor sizes. Appendix E specifies different planning horizons, temperatures, discounts, and reward thresholds for these tests. Figure 3 also replaces the displayed LSTM K-Means condition with VAE, and Figure 2 adds an EC reset control.

E4.justification: Appendices H.2–H.3 introduce substantial analyses of scalability, memory growth with experience, and robustness to an irrelevant noisy variable. Figures 10–12 test these questions directly. The original clean-input factor-size analysis and Dreamer experiment remain; their relocation is not an additional analysis.

E5.justification: Both versions specify five experiments with different seeds. V4 clarifies that one standard deviation is shown except for boxplots, qualifying v3's blanket standard-deviation statement. This is a limited reporting clarification, without evidence of increased repeated-run counts or new statistical tests.

E6.justification: V4 adds RWKV, oracle-EC, and EC-VAE outcomes. New Figures 10–11 show fewer DHTM memory units during goal-directed learning but more than EC under uniform exploration, with approximately linear growth versus episode length. Figure 12 shows noise tolerance for smaller DHTM factors and failure for EC and factor-6 DHTM. The original factor-size and Dreamer findings are retained.

T1.justification: New Appendix G assumes uniformly sampled categorical features, derives a collision-based capacity expression in Equation 18, and argues for linear scaling with neuron count using a Taylor expansion. This adds a substantive theoretical argument absent from v3. Existing DHTM and value-decomposition derivations are retained or relocated; Section 2.1 also corrects the Q-function discount exponent.

C1.justification: The central contributions—online Hebbian episodic memory, successor-feature planning, and distributed representations—remain unchanged. V4 extends the abstract and introduction's comparative claim to RWKV and adds a qualified novelty claim concerning episodic control in partially observable environments. The conclusion's principal claims remain stable.

C2.justification: V4 adds substantive explanations of why factorization tolerates noisy features and why including all variables loses that advantage. Appendix H.2 discusses exploration-dependent memory growth, unstable policies in larger grids, linear computational costs, and planning-horizon limitations requiring pruning or alternative planning approaches. These considerably sharpen v3's broader limitations discussion.

D1.justification: V4 documents segment-creation conditions, KL-based stopping, RWKV implementation and training, EC's VAE mapping, and parameters for the scalability and noise experiments. It replaces the anonymous code reference with a named GitHub repository and iclr25 branch. Conversely, it removes the explicit statement that the oracle-CSCG buffer continuously grows, without specifying a replacement behavior.

R1.justification: V4 substantially expands positioning around cognitive maps versus episodic memory and compares DHTM conceptually with asymmetric Hopfield networks, temporal predictive coding, and HTM. It adds corresponding literature and a probabilistic-HTM interpretation, replaces the earlier Hawkins framework citation with Hawkins and Ahmad (2016), and removes the Blundell episodic-control citation. These exceed bibliographic or citation-style changes.

P1.justification: V4 substantially rewrites background and neural-implementation explanations, moves the detailed neuronal derivation into Appendix B, and incorporates the former episodic-control background into Section 3.5. The introduction's narrative is expanded and reorganized. These structural and explanatory revisions go beyond the accompanying new scientific content.

P2.justification: V4 adopts ICLR formatting, revises Figures 2–3 and their legends, labels the Gridworld maps more explicitly, and adds Figures 7 and 10–12 for scaling environments, memory growth, and noise tolerance. Existing biological diagrams and the Dreamer plot are retained or relocated, rather than newly introduced.

improvement.justification: V4 substantially strengthens evidence for DHTM's advantages and limits relative to episodic control. V3's AnimalAI EC comparison used K-Means; v4 adds EC with VAE encoding, a noisy-feature test, and controlled scalability and memory-growth analyses. Together with RWKV comparisons and clearer implementation details, these address important gaps in comparative validity and reproducibility. The new analyses also expose instability and resource costs instead of presenting uniformly favorable results. Simple navigation environments and the simplifying assumptions of the capacity argument still limit generality.
